title: Union-find, tries and longest prefix match: concepts
seriesDescription: Language-independent interview topics (concepts, SQL, design, AI engineering): no Java and no Python code or library names.
description: Union-find with rank and path compression, counting components, redundant connection, tries and IP-style longest prefix matching, without language-specific code.
source: CLRS ch. 19-21; cp-algorithms DSU; LeetCode Redundant Connection, Implement Trie, Word Search II; RFC 4632 (CIDR); Princeton Algorithms (Sedgewick)

questions.prompt: Start with 8 separate nodes 0..7 and process unions in this order: (0,1), (1,2), (3,4), (5,6), (6,7), (2,0), (4,5). How many connected components remain?
questions.explanation: Six of the seven calls merge two different sets (8 - 6 = 2); (2,0) is redundant because 0, 1, 2 are already together. Final sets: {0,1,2} and {3,4,5,6,7}.

questions.prompt: With union by rank and path compression, what is the amortised cost of one find or union?
questions.explanation: Interview answer: "nearly constant amortised, O(alpha(n))". Either optimisation alone gives O(log n) amortised.

options.text: O(log n) worst case per find, because rank only bounds the height of each tree.
options.why: Rank alone gives that bound; adding path compression improves it further.

options.text: O(1) worst case for every single find.
options.why: A single find can still walk a path; only the amortised cost is near-constant.

options.text: O(alpha(n)), the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant.
options.why: Correct: the combined optimisations give a near-constant amortised bound.

options.text: O(n) per find, since a chain can still form.
options.why: Union by rank prevents chains, so tree height stays O(log n).

questions.explanation: Union by rank alone gives O(log n) trees. Add path compression and the amortised cost drops to O(alpha(n)).
questions.text: Union by {1} attaches the shallower tree under the deeper root, keeping height O({2} n); path {3} re-points visited nodes straight at the root.

questions.prompt: You add the edges of an undirected graph one at a time.
questions.explanation: This is the core of Redundant Connection and Kruskal's MST. For directed graphs it does not apply directly; use DFS colouring or topological sort.
questions.assertion: Union-find can detect that an added edge closes a cycle.
questions.reason: If both endpoints already have the same root, they are already connected, so the new edge forms a cycle.

whys.a: Right: R is exactly the test used (union returns false).
whys.b: R is the mechanism that makes A true.

questions.prompt: Kruskal's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree.
questions.explanation: Sorting costs O(E log E) and dominates. The greedy rule "cheapest edge that does not close a cycle" needs both parts.
questions.assertion: Kruskal's algorithm starts by sorting the edges by weight.
questions.reason: A union-find structure answers whether two vertices are already connected.

whys.a: R is a separate tool; it does not explain why sorting comes first.
whys.b: Right: both are true; the sort supplies the cheapest-first order and union-find supplies the cycle test, two different ingredients.

questions.explanation: Rank alone gives O(log n) per operation; compression alone gives O(log n) amortised; both give O(alpha(n)).
questions.assertion: Union by rank alone keeps every tree at O(log n) height.
questions.reason: Without path compression, a union-find structure is no better than a linked list.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: rank alone bounds height by log n, so even without compression a structure is far better than a list; R is false.

questions.prompt: True or false: a standard union-find can efficiently undo a union, so edges can be deleted one at a time.
questions.explanation: Interview trick: if edges are removed, process the operations in reverse and turn deletions into unions. A rollback union-find (union by size, no path compression, with an undo stack) can undo the most recent unions in LIFO order, but arbitrary deletion is not supported.

options.text: True
options.why: Standard union-find with path compression has no way to split a set again.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: it supports merging only; deletions need a different approach.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which problems are naturally solved with union-find?
questions.explanation: Union-find answers "are these two connected?" and "how many groups?", nothing about distances or order.

options.text: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree.
options.why: Correct: the cycle test is a find on both endpoints.

options.text: Finding the shortest weighted path from one source.
options.why: Union-find knows connectivity, not distances; use Dijkstra.

options.text: Merging accounts that share an email address.
options.why: Correct: shared emails union the accounts into groups.

options.text: Producing a topological order of a DAG.
options.why: Ordering needs in-degrees or DFS, not set merging.

questions.prompt: Insert car, cart, cat, dog and do into an empty trie. How many nodes exist excluding the root?
questions.explanation: Shared prefixes are stored once: c-a-r (3), t under r for cart (4), t under a for cat (5), d-o-g (8); "do" reuses d-o. Including the root that would be 9.

questions.prompt: A router table has 0.0.0.0/0, 10.0.0.0/8, 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.1.2.0/24. A packet arrives for 10.1.3.7. What is the prefix length of the entry chosen by longest-prefix match?
questions.explanation: 10.1.3.7 is inside /0, /8 and /16, but not 10.1.2.0/24 (third octet is 3, not 2). The longest matching prefix is /16.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement with the data structure that fits best.
questions.explanation: A trie walks the prefix in O(L) and lists the subtree; a binary trie over the 32 address bits finds the deepest route on the path; a hash table gives O(1) exact lookup; an ordered map gives floor/ceiling; a Bloom filter may report false positives but never false negatives.

left.text: Autocomplete: all words with a given prefix
IP routing: longest matching CIDR prefix
Exact key lookup, no ordering needed
Keys in sorted order with floor and ceiling queries
Approximate membership with no false negatives

right.text: Binary trie keyed on address bits

questions.prompt: A teammate proposes storing every route in a hash table keyed by "address/length".
questions.explanation: Hash-per-length tables are used in software, but real routers use tries or TCAM. Say both and the trade-offs.
questions.assertion: A single hash lookup is enough to find the longest matching prefix for a packet.
questions.reason: A trie finds it in one walk over the address bits, remembering the deepest node that holds a route.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: a hash table must be probed once per candidate length (up to 32 times for IPv4); the trie does it in one pass, so R is true while A is false.

questions.prompt: You build a trie for autocompleting search terms in many languages (a huge, sparse alphabet). How should each node store its children?
questions.explanation: Array children give O(1) indexed access for a small known alphabet (e.g. lowercase letters); hash tables win for Unicode.

options.text: A hash table from character to child, since most characters never occur at a node.
options.why: Correct: memory grows with the children that exist, not with the alphabet size.

options.text: A fixed array with one slot per possible character in every node, because arrays always use less memory.
options.why: With a huge alphabet almost every slot would be empty, wasting memory.

options.text: A sorted list scanned linearly at every node.
options.why: Scanning a long list at each level slows lookups far beyond O(L).

options.text: A single global table from full word to node, with no per-node children.
options.why: That loses the shared-prefix structure and the prefix queries a trie exists for.

questions.prompt: Edges of an undirected graph arrive in this order: (1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (1,4), (1,5). Counting from 1, which edge is the first that closes a cycle?
questions.explanation: After the first three edges nodes 1-4 are in one set, so (1,4) joins two nodes with the same root. This is Redundant Connection: the union returns false on that edge. (1,5) later attaches a new node.

questions.prompt: In Word Search II (find many words in a grid), why build a trie of the words instead of running Word Search I once per word?
questions.explanation: Typical optimisation: store the full word at the end node, clear it once found to avoid duplicates, and prune trie leaves after a match. This is among the most commonly asked trie questions.

options.text: The trie sorts the words, so the grid can be searched with binary search.
options.why: Grid search is a DFS over neighbours; sorted words do not enable binary search on it.

options.text: The trie removes the need to mark visited cells during the DFS.
options.why: A path may still not reuse a cell, so visited marking is needed.

options.text: The trie makes every cell visit O(1) and the total cost independent of the grid size.
options.why: The grid still has to be traversed; the trie only cuts repeated and hopeless work.

options.text: One DFS walks the grid and the trie together and stops when the path is no prefix.
options.why: Correct: shared prefixes are explored once and dead paths are pruned early.

questions.prompt: Complete the description of Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm.
questions.explanation: Sorting dominates, so the total is O(E log E) = O(E log V). Prim's algorithm with a heap reaches the same bound; Kruskal's find step is the same cycle test as in Redundant Connection.
questions.text: Sort the edges by {1}; take an edge only if its endpoints have different {2} in the union-find; stop after {3} edges for a graph with n vertices.

questions.prompt: True or false: looking up a word in a trie takes time proportional to the word's length, not to the number of words stored.
questions.explanation: That is O(L) per lookup, which is why tries suit prefix queries on huge dictionaries. The price is memory for the nodes.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the walk follows one node per character regardless of how many words exist.

options.text: False
options.why: The lookup never scans other words, so the statement is true.

questions.prompt: Write pseudocode for find(x) with path compression and union(a, b) with union by rank. union must return false if a and b are already connected and true otherwise.
questions.explanation: The boolean return is what makes Redundant Connection and cycle detection one line. Path halving or an iterative find are equally good. Any pseudocode with the same logic is acceptable.

checks.label: find re-points the node to its root (path compression)
union returns false when the roots are equal

questions.model:
find(x):
    if parent[x] != x: parent[x] = find(parent[x])
    return parent[x]

union(a, b):
    ra = find(a); rb = find(b)
    if ra == rb: return false
    if rank[ra] < rank[rb]: swap(ra, rb)
    parent[rb] = ra
    if rank[ra] == rank[rb]: rank[ra] = rank[ra] + 1
    return true
